ABOUT THE APP

Hey Reachy is a network client for the Reachy Mini desktop robots from Pollen
Robotics. It is an independent client, not affiliated with Pollen Robotics. The
app speaks to the robot's own HTTP and WebSocket daemon.

DEMO VIDEO - VERSION 0.5.0 (204) ON A PHYSICAL iPHONE

The video is attached to this section: Hey-Reachy-0.5.0-demo.mp4

A Reachy Mini Wireless robot is in the same frame. This video replaces the
previous one and is valid for all storefronts.

0:00  The app starts from the Home Screen.
0:05  The "Before you start" screen.
0:09  The app finds the robot over Bluetooth.
0:13  The Connect screen pairs with the robot.
0:17  The Robot tab: the link, the state and the motor power.
0:21  The Moves tab. 0:25 the Settings tab and the audio levels.
0:30  The Live tab wakes the robot and opens the camera.
0:36  The microphone permission request.
0:51  CALL START. The user unmutes the microphone. The call controls appear.
0:53  The app goes to the background. The green call pill is beside the clock.
0:57  The app returns to the front. The call is still active.
1:00  The red button in the app ends the call.
1:03  The Phone app. The Recents list holds the robot. A tap calls it again.

CALL SERVICES - WHAT THE APP USES

The app carries two-way voice with the robot. The user speaks, the robot plays
the voice through its speaker, and the robot's microphone comes back. The app
presents that session as a system call through LiveCommunicationKit, which is
the successor to CallKit.

The app starts calls. It never receives them. A call always goes out to a robot
that the user owns. No other person can call this app, so the app registers no
VoIP push and never reports an incoming call. The "voip" background mode is what
entitles ConversationManager to perform a call transaction. Without that mode
the framework refuses the transaction.

These are all the call services the app supports:
- Start a call, from the microphone button.
- Mute and unmute during a call.
- End a call, from the red button in the app.
- Donate the call to Recents, so the Phone app can call the robot again.

HOW iOS DRAWS THIS CALL

iOS gives a call from an app other than FaceTime one compact pill beside the
clock. The pill does not expand and it carries no buttons. iOS also hides the
pill while the app is in the foreground. So the video puts the app in the
background to show it. The user ends the call in the app, because the system
shows no End button for such a call.

DEMO ACCOUNT

The Hugging Face sign-in gives one function: remote access to a robot that is
linked to that account. The sign-in is optional. All other functions work
without an account.

The demo account has no robot linked to it. A robot is hardware, and we cannot
send you one. After you sign in, the "Your Reachies" screen shows "No Reachy
online". This is the correct result. No other content is behind the sign-in.

To sign in: select the "HF" segment on the Connect screen. Tap "Your Reachies".
Tap "Sign in". Use the account name and the password in this section.

HOW TO REVIEW THE APP WITHOUT A ROBOT

The app carries a simulator of the control path. It needs no robot, no account,
no network and no permission.

1. On the Connect screen, select the "Simulator" segment.
2. Tap "Start the simulator".
3. The app builds a robot from its own description and opens the main tabs.

The simulator answers the Live tab, the Robot tab and Settings. It declines the
camera, the two-way audio, the app catalogue, the moves, the soundboard and the
Wi-Fi setup. Each one belongs to a physical machine.

FIRST LAUNCH

A Bluetooth sheet opens over the Connect screen at the first launch. Dismiss it
with Cancel. The iOS Local Network alert waits below it. Allow it, or select the
"Simulator" segment, which needs no permission.
EOF

#!/bin/sh
# =============================================================================
# Keep SwiftPM off a beta Xcode's SDK — sourced, never executed
# =============================================================================
# The swift.org toolchain pinned in `.swift-version` cannot read every SDK a beta
# Xcode ships. Swift 6.3.0 against Xcode 27 beta's macOS 27 SDK puts the backing
# storage of a `@State private` property into the synthesised memberwise
# initialiser, which makes that initialiser private too. ReachyUI then refuses to
# compile at 401 call sites across ten types — this line first said thirteen, which
# was the count before anyone re-measured it (`docs/research/ios-27.md`):
#
#     error: 'LogConsoleView' initializer is inaccessible due to
#     'private' protection level
#
# The same source builds green under Xcode 27's own Swift 6.4 and on CI, whose
# `lint-test` job runs SwiftPM on an image with a release SDK. So this is the SDK,
# not the code, and the machine already carries a release SDK beside the beta one:
# the Command Line Tools ship theirs at a path of their own.
#
# Only while a beta Xcode is selected. The override removes itself the day the
# release arrives, and it does nothing on Linux, where `xcode-select` is absent.
# Case-folded: Apple ships `Xcode-beta.app` and Xcodes.app names the same build
# `Xcode-27.0.0-Beta.6.app`, so matching one spelling silently misses the other.
#
# **And only for a swift.org toolchain, which is what the paragraph above is about.**
# Xcode's own Swift reads the beta SDK perfectly well — `swift build` against Xcode 27
# beta 6's macOS 27 SDK completes in 32 s here, the same configuration `lint-test`
# builds in — so swapping the SDK out from under a machine with no swiftly installed
# bought nothing and cost the one thing #124 needed: a `Sources/` that names an iOS 27
# symbol cannot compile against a 26.5 SDK, so every local `mise run build` and
# `mise run test` would fail over declarations the four app jobs build happily.
#
# A swift.org toolchain keeps the swap, and now for a second reason as well as the
# first: it cannot build this package against either SDK any more — 27 symbols are
# absent from 26.5 — and "cannot find 'LongRunningIntent' in scope" is a far better
# thing to read than 401 inaccessible-initialiser errors across ten types.
#
# The version line is the measurement rather than a path guess: Xcode's toolchain
# stamps `swiftlang-6.4.0.33.1`, a swift.org build stamps `swift-6.3.3-RELEASE`.
case "$(xcode-select -p 2>/dev/null | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')" in
*beta*)
	if [ -z "${SDKROOT:-}" ] &&
		[ -d /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/SDKs/MacOSX.sdk ] &&
		! swift --version 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'swiftlang-'; then
		SDKROOT=/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/SDKs/MacOSX.sdk
		export SDKROOT
	fi
	;;
esac

content.content:
# Discovery & local networking

## Discovery (lessons from upstream issue #269)

Upstream discovery loops forever when mDNS returns several addresses for one robot (IPv4 from different subnets,
link-local IPv6). Our rules:

- Identify a robot by `GET /api/daemon/hardware-id`, never by IP.
- Store the last successful address; manual IP entry is a first-class feature, not a fallback.
- Show the user which address is in use; provide a force-reconnect action.
- Build URLs with `URLComponents` (brackets IPv6 correctly). Drop `fe80::` link-local candidates unless carrying a
  zone ID.
- Connect must be idempotent and cancellable — no latching state machines.
- Static fallback host: `reachy-mini.local`. Upstream also probes `reachy-mini.home`; do NOT add it back. ATS waives
  its HTTPS requirement only for `.local` names, link-local addresses and single-label hosts, so a qualified `.home`
  name is always refused with `NSURLErrorDomain -1022` — confirmed on a running build. Loopback is probed as well on
  macOS and in the simulator, which is the path that does not depend on discovery working.
- `sim-daemon` **does** advertise `_reachy-mini._tcp`, and a simulator on the same Mac lists it — verified by
  connecting to one from the simulator. A stand-in advert for discovery work is one command:
  `dns-sd -R reachy_mini _reachy-mini._tcp local 8000 unit_id=<hex>`, and a second registration of the same instance
  name comes back as `reachy_mini (2)`.
- An empty discovery list says nothing about the app. Check the robot is actually up first (`ping`, `arp -n <ip>`,
  `dns-sd -B _reachy-mini._tcp`) — a robot that dropped off the network stops advertising, and every layer above
  correctly reports nothing.
- Network change: `NWPathMonitor` + exponential backoff reconnect.

## macOS sandbox (app target)

- **WebRTC needs `com.apple.security.network.server`, not only `network.client`.** ICE binds UDP sockets and receives
  datagrams from a peer it never `connect()`ed to, which App Sandbox counts as inbound; without the key the bind is
  refused *before* the firewall is consulted, so nothing prompts and nothing logs. The stream then never leaves
  `.connecting` and `CameraSession`'s 10 s watchdog renegotiates for ever — which reads as "the camera does not turn
  on" rather than as a permission. The tell that the app really does listen is macOS asking "accept incoming network
  connections?" once the entitlement is there.
- **An empty ICE candidate is the end-of-candidates marker**, and the robot's gstreamer webrtcsink sends one on every
  negotiation. `RTCIceCandidate.init` answers it with `NSParameterAssert(sdp.length)` — an `NSException`, which no
  `try?` catches, thrown by an argument evaluated before `peerConnection?.add` is reached. `CameraSession+ICE.swift`
  is the one guard, and it covers the LAN and the relay alike because both signalling paths funnel into it.

## iOS/iPadOS requirements (app targets)

- `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` + `NSBonjourServices` in Info.plist. Daemon mDNS service types (from upstream
  `src-tauri/src/discovery/mod.rs`): `_reachy-mini._tcp` (primary) and `_http._tcp` (legacy, filter instance names
  containing "reachy") — declare both.
- Local Network permission denial is SILENT: discovery returns an empty list, no error. UX must explain before the
  prompt, detect denial via timeout, and deep-link to Settings.
- ATS: `NSAppTransportSecurity → NSAllowsLocalNetworking: true` — allows plain HTTP to `.local`/link-local only. Never
  use blanket `NSExceptionDomains`.
- The daemon transport is plaintext and unauthenticated. Support only trusted private LANs or the robot AP; show this
  limitation in connection UI and never encourage public routing/port forwarding.

## Robot facts

- Wireless AP mode (out of box): SSID `reachy-mini-ap`, password `reachy-mini`, robot IP `10.42.0.1`.
- BLE Wi-Fi provisioning, daemon 1.9.0+. Upstream doc:
  `reachy_mini/src/reachy_mini/daemon/app/services/bluetooth/BLE_WIFI_PROVISIONING.md` (maps to CryptoKit X25519 +
  HKDF-SHA256 + AES-GCM). The authority is `bluetooth_service.py` beside it, not the doc — **the doc is wrong about
  replies.** It claims every command notifies, but `CommandCharacteristic.WriteValue` assigns the response value
  directly; only daemon-proxied commands notify, after an `OK: working` ack. So: write → read → await a notification
  only if the read was that ack. Awaiting unconditionally hangs on `PING`.
- The robot advertises the **status** service `…cdef3`, not the command service `…cdef0`, under the local name
  `ReachyMini` — identical on every unit, so robots are told apart only after connecting, by `…cdef7`.
  - **The advertisement carries no `ManufacturerData` at all** — measured on a Wireless unit on 2026-08-13, on a
    build that keeps the field across sightings and scans with `allowDuplicates`, so the absence is the robot's and
    not the scanner's. Upstream PR #1086 puts a flag, an IPv4 address and seven bytes of the hardware id under
    company `0xFFFF`; this firmware predates it. `BLEAdvertisement` decodes that shape and answers nil here, and the
    recovery console prints the raw bytes so the next measurement costs a glance rather than a build. **Do not plan
    on identifying robots before connecting until that row shows something.**
  - Two things had to be fixed before the measurement meant anything, and either alone makes a robot that advertises
    look exactly like one that does not: `merging` replaced the whole snapshot, so a sighting without the block
    erased one that had it — CoreBluetooth calls back per packet and the block usually rides the scan response — and
    the scan asked for no duplicates, which lets iOS coalesce a peripheral into a single callback that may never

  correctly reports nothing.
- Network change: `NWPathMonitor` + exponential backoff reconnect.

## macOS sandbox (app target)

- **WebRTC needs `com.apple.security.network.server`, not only `network.client`.** ICE binds UDP sockets and receives
  datagrams from a peer it never `connect()`ed to, which App Sandbox counts as inbound; without the key the bind is
  refused *before* the firewall is consulted, so nothing prompts and nothing logs. The stream then never leaves
  `.connecting` and `CameraSession`'s 10 s watchdog renegotiates for ever — which reads as "the camera does not turn
  on" rather than as a permission. The tell that the app really does listen is macOS asking "accept incoming network
  connections?" once the entitlement is there.

  negotiation. `RTCIceCandidate.init` answers it with `NSParameterAssert(sdp.length)` — an `NSException`, which no
  `try?` catches, thrown by an argument evaluated before `peerConnection?.add` is reached. `CameraSession+ICE.swift`

ABOUT THE APP

Hey Reachy is a network client for the Reachy Mini desktop robots from Pollen
Robotics. It is an independent client, not affiliated with Pollen Robotics. The
app speaks to the robot's own HTTP and WebSocket daemon.

ACCOUNT DELETION (5.1.1(v))

The app creates no account. It has no server and no user database. The only
sign-in is OAuth into an existing Hugging Face account that the user already
owns. The app holds one access token in the iOS Keychain, and "Sign out" deletes
that token from the device.

Version 0.5.0 (205) adds a direct link to the page where the user deletes that
Hugging Face account:

  Settings tab > "Hugging Face" section > "Delete your Hugging Face account"

The row appears as soon as the user signs in, below the account row. It opens
https://huggingface.co/settings/account, which carries the "Delete my account"
control.

DEMO VIDEO - VERSION 0.5.0 ON A PHYSICAL iPHONE

The video is attached to this section: Hey-Reachy-0.5.0-demo.mp4

A Reachy Mini Wireless robot is in the same frame. The video is valid for all
storefronts.

0:00 the app starts. 0:09 it finds the robot over Bluetooth. 0:13 the Connect
screen pairs. 0:17 the Robot tab. 0:21 Moves. 0:25 Settings. 0:30 the Live tab
opens the camera. 0:36 the microphone permission request. 0:51 CALL START, from
the microphone button. 0:53 the app goes to the background and the green call
pill shows beside the clock. 0:57 the app returns. 1:00 the red button ends the
call. 1:03 the Phone app: Recents holds the robot, and a tap calls it again.

CALL SERVICES

The app carries two-way voice with the robot, and presents it as a system call
through LiveCommunicationKit, the successor to CallKit. The app starts calls. It
never receives them, so it registers no VoIP push. The "voip" background mode is
what entitles ConversationManager to perform a call transaction.

All the call services: start a call from the microphone button; mute and unmute
during a call; end a call from the red button; donate the call to Recents.

iOS gives a call from an app other than FaceTime one compact pill beside the
clock. The pill does not expand and carries no buttons, and iOS hides it while
the app is in the foreground. The user ends the call in the app, because the
system shows no End button for such a call.

DEMO ACCOUNT

The Hugging Face sign-in gives one function: remote access to a robot linked to
that account. It is optional. All other functions work without an account.

The demo account has no robot linked to it. A robot is hardware, and we cannot
send you one. After you sign in, "Your Reachies" shows "No Reachy online". This
is the correct result. No other content is behind the sign-in.

To sign in: select the "HF" segment on the Connect screen. Tap "Your Reachies",
then "Sign in". Use the account in this section.

HOW TO REVIEW WITHOUT A ROBOT

The app carries a simulator of the control path. It needs no robot, no account,
no network and no permission.

1. On the Connect screen, select the "Simulator" segment.
2. Tap "Start the simulator".
3. The app builds a robot from its own description and opens the main tabs.

The simulator answers the Live tab, the Robot tab and Settings. It declines the
camera, the two-way audio, the app catalogue, the moves and the Wi-Fi setup.
Each one belongs to a physical machine.

FIRST LAUNCH

A Bluetooth sheet opens over the Connect screen. Dismiss it with Cancel. The iOS
Local Network alert waits below it. Allow it, or select "Simulator", which needs
no permission.

a throwaway-account recording if they insist.

What it cost: build 205, and **20 reference images** — `HFAccountPreviewsTests`, five scenes × two
devices × two appearances. Nothing else moved, which also proved Xcode 27.0 GM renders identically to
the beta the earlier references were recorded on.

while the user is signed in. It opens huggingface.co/settings/account, which
carries the "Delete my account" control.

appearances. Nothing else moved, which also shows that Xcode 27.0 renders the
references the same way the beta did.
